item.title: What You Can Build with Brakeza3D, and Using It with AI Agents
item.description: What projects suit Brakeza3D, an open source C++ game engine with Lua, and why its text formats and command-line tests work well with AI coding agents.
item.content:encoded:
Two questions keep coming up in messages: what is Brakeza3D good for? and can I use it with Claude, Copilot or other coding agents? This post answers both, because the answers are connected.

What kind of projects suit Brakeza3D​

Brakeza3D is a free, open source engine written in C++ (OpenGL, deferred rendering, Bullet physics, Lua scripting, GLSL and node-based shaders, integrated editor). It is built for small and medium real-time projects, not for a studio shipping a 100-person AAA game. In practice, that covers:

  • Prototypes and game jams. Open the editor, drop in a model, attach a Lua script, press play. No recompiling the engine to try an idea.
  • Strategy and simulation games. Candelabra, a city-sized RTS with hundreds of units, civilians, traffic, police and a day/night cycle, runs on it. It is also the hardest test the engine has had, and it keeps pushing the engine forward.
  • 3D action and exploration games with physics, lighting, particles and animated characters. The tutorial project in the engine shows each piece in isolation: physics, characters, particles and crowds, UI, audio and video, shaders.
  • Visual experiments and shader work. The node-based shader editor and GLSL support make it a comfortable sandbox for graphics programming.
  • Learning. The whole engine is readable C++ with a documented Lua API, so you can follow a feature from the script down to the renderer.

What it is not: a drop-in replacement for the largest commercial engines, with their asset stores and console toolchains. If you want full control over the pipeline and a small, understandable codebase, it fits.

Why it works well with AI agents​

I did not design Brakeza3D around AI. But a lot of the choices that make an engine pleasant for a human who likes plain files turn out to be exactly what a coding agent needs.

1. Almost everything is text. Projects, scenes and game data are JSON. Gameplay is Lua. Shaders are GLSL. There is no opaque binary project format between the agent and your game: it reads a file, changes a file, and you can review the change in git like any other.

2. The scripting API is documented. The Scripting API covers objects, physics, sound, shaders, UI widgets and more, and the engine's own source tree has a project instruction file for agents (CLAUDE.md) describing the architecture, the frame loop order and the conventions to follow. An agent that reads it starts with the same map I use.

3. Lua means fast feedback. An agent can write a script, run the game and look at the result without a C++ build in the loop. When it does need to touch the engine, the code follows the conventions described in that instruction file.

4. Command-line parameters turn the game into a test. A project can declare parameters that you pass at launch with --set name=value. In Candelabra I use them for scenario tests: spawn 200 units against 200, run for a fixed time, exit, write a report to a log file. An agent can launch that, read the report and decide the next step, with no human clicking in the editor.

5. The engine can measure itself. There is a built-in profiler exposed to Lua, so a script can collect CPU and GPU time per phase, draw calls and per-script cost and write them as text. An agent that can read numbers can tell whether its change helped.

A real example​

I used an AI agent on exactly that loop to optimize the 200 vs 200 battle in Candelabra. The agent profiled the scenario, found that every bullet created a physical object with a script, replaced straight bullets with a targeted-hit model, capped the visual effects, and lowered the update rate of systems that did not need one. In the steady scenario the frame went from about 205 ms to about 117-124 ms, in measured steps, and every change was a reviewable commit. It also made mistakes along the way (a wrong guess about where time went, an optimization that gave no gain and was reverted), and the measurements are what caught them. That is the real point: the engine gives the agent a way to check its own work.

Getting started with an agent​

  1. Download the engine or clone the repository.
  2. Open the repository in your agent of choice, and point it at CLAUDE.md and the Scripting API documentation.
  3. Start with a small task: a script that moves an object, a new shader, a UI widget.
  4. Ask it to run the project with a command-line parameter and to read the log, not just to write code.

The pattern that has worked best for me: small tasks, a way to run the result, and a number or a log to check it against. Brakeza3D makes the second and third easy.

If you build something with it, I would like to see it: the gallery and the Assets Hub are open to the community.

item.title: A strategy game is not made of code alone: the RTS Editor
item.description: The RTS Editor: the HTML tool used to manage quests, NPCs, dialogue, units and translated strings of the Candelabra RTS built on the Brakeza3D engine.
item.content:encoded:
How a single HTML file became the tool that keeps a 27-quest RTS, 35 unit types and 869 translated strings standing, and how I ended up handing it to people who never touch code.

When people talk about making a game they talk about the engine, the shaders, the physics. Almost never about what takes the most hours: entering and maintaining data. In Candelabra, the RTS I am building on Brakeza3D, every quest, every dialogue line, every building cost and every unit lives in a JSON file. Editing that by hand works for the first ten days. After that it stops working.

This post is about the RTS Editor: why I built it, what it does today, and what I learned. The thesis is simple: tools are not a luxury of big projects; they are what lets a project grow without falling apart.

The start screen: project counters (27 quests, 20 NPCs, 35 unit types, 25 tech nodes, 298 building assignments) and the city map with civilian and traffic routes.

The problem: data everywhere​

The game reads dozens of JSON files: quests, NPCs and their dialogue trees, unit types, building types, interiors, routes, facade windows, UI text in two languages... The problems show up quickly:

  • Fragile cross references. A quest mentions an NPC, who mentions a building, which unlocks a technology. A misspelled identifier does not raise an error: the quest simply never completes.
  • Spatial data. You cannot write the entry point of an interior by eye. You have to see it on the map.
  • Size. With 298 building assignments or 869 strings, searching and comparing by hand is a guaranteed source of mistakes.

The solution: one HTML file, no server, no install​

The editor is a single page (about 12,000 lines) that opens in Chrome or Edge. It uses the File System Access API: you press "Open Project Folder", pick the project root, and the editor reads and writes the JSON files directly. No backend, no build step, no dependencies.

That has a benefit that is not obvious at first: what the editor edits is exactly the files in the repository. There is no intermediate database and no export step. A change in the editor is a change in git diff, reviewed and reverted like any other.

It also writes files with exactly the formatting the existing ones have, so saving a file you did not touch produces no diff at all. I checked that round-tripping the existing files is byte-identical, because a tool that adds noise to every commit gets abandoned.

A tour of the useful parts​

Quests: forms instead of JSON​

A quest has objectives, prerequisites, a chain, a time limit and a failure branch. The form knows the objective types (reach a resource amount, kill, talk, enter a building...) and offers only the fields that apply to each. Effects on accept, complete and fail (give resources, unlock a contact, send a phone message, start a call, play a cinematic...) are picked from a list with their own fields. A JSON Preview tab shows the exact result.

Dialogues: a graph, not a text tree​

Dialogues branch, get locked depending on quest state (the padlock on an option) and loop back. Nested JSON is unreadable; a node graph is not. You drag nodes, click an option to jump to its target, and "Auto Layout" tidies everything when the tree gets messy.

Tech tree: seeing the dependencies​

Each technology has a cost, a required building, prerequisites and unlocks. The Tree View tab draws them as a graph, so an orphan node or an over-long chain is obvious at a glance.

Interiors: spatial data, on the map​

An interior needs an entry point, an exit point, a minimap image and a pathfinding image (the green area units can walk on). The editor shows both images next to the fields and lets you drag the points on the map. This is where a visual tool beats editing numbers by a mile. Interior items and their actions (look, take, read, show a photo...) are edited here too.

Buildings and units: balance without touching code​

The assignments table links every submesh of the map to a faction and a building type, with filters and bulk edits. The unit sheet gathers damage, range, health, speed, model, script, avatar and lifecycle. Tuning the balance becomes a matter of minutes and needs no recompile.

General configuration​

Global parameters (shadows, selection circles, UI scale...) have their own section. The project rule is that every new parameter goes both into the game's config file and into this screen, so nobody has to hunt for a constant buried in a .lua.

Translations: 869 strings, two languages​

The editor collects every string in the game (dialogues, quests, UI, technologies), shows it in two columns (original and translation), marks each one as pending, machine-translated, reviewed or outdated, lets you filter, and imports and exports CSV to work outside. When you edit the Spanish source text, the English translation of that string flips to outdated by itself, so nothing silently drifts out of sync. This is the part that saves the most time and prevents the most mistakes.

Road graph​

City traffic runs on a lane graph (97 nodes, 419 lanes and 110 crosswalks on the full map). The editor overlays it on the map so you can fix lanes, traffic lights and junctions. It even warns that the city graph is generated by a script and that manual changes are lost if it is regenerated: a warning in the exact place where it matters.

The latest additions: the story's loose ends​

For a long time the editor covered quests, dialogues and numbers, but not the small pieces of text that make a world feel inhabited. Those lived in JSON files you edited by hand, and they were the first thing to get stale. Three new sections fixed that:

  • Calls. A phone call is a linear dialogue: who rings, whether the incoming-call screen appears, what happens if you decline (drop it, ring again every N seconds with a retry limit, or make it impossible to decline) and the lines. Lines can be reordered, and a call that is never answered can send a "missed call" text message.
  • SMS. The message catalogue (an id, a sender, the text and the contact it unlocks) and the initial inbox the player starts with.
  • Barks. The loose phrases NPCs shout on the street, grouped by situation: idle, hero nearby, quest available, quest done.

They share the same data objects as the translations panel, so editing a phrase immediately marks its English version as outdated, and they keep any field the form does not know about when saving. The validator learned about them too: a duplicated SMS id, an inbox entry that points to a message that does not exist, or a quest effect that calls a file that is not there, now show up as warnings before saving.

Images, without leaving the editor​

Lore is also pictures: a photo on a desk, a letter, a portrait. The editor now has an image manager: browse the game's images by folder with thumbnails, upload new ones, replace an existing one keeping its name (so no reference breaks), delete, and copy the path ready to paste into a JSON file. Before replacing or deleting anything it saves the previous version aside, so nothing is ever lost. Character portraits and the big chat avatars use the same mechanism straight from the NPC sheet.

Handing it to people who do not write code​

The best test of a tool is giving it to someone else. I built a frozen copy: one folder containing only the data, the editor and a short guide, with a double-click launcher that opens it in Chrome or Edge, another that zips the work to send back, and an optional checker that finds broken links between quests, dialogues and flags. The people writing the story open the folder in the editor, write, and send me a zip. They never see a line of code, and before every save the editor warns about the things it knows are wrong.

It is a copy on purpose: the story writers work against a snapshot, and I merge their changes by hand. It costs me a few minutes per delivery and it removes any chance of two people overwriting each other's files.

Safety nets​

An editor that lets more people touch the data needs more ways to catch mistakes:

  • The editor's own validator runs before saving and lists missing quests, unknown effects, unreachable dialogue nodes and the new SMS and call checks above. It warns; it never blocks.
  • A standalone lore checker walks the whole story: broken links between quests, NPCs and phone messages, flags nobody sets, quests nobody offers or finishes, cycles, and whether there is an ending.
  • A quest simulator runs the quest logic against a fake engine, so a change that breaks the main chain can fail a test instead of a playthrough.

What I learned​

  1. Build the tool when it hurts, not before and not much later. The first quest form paid for itself within days.
  2. Edit the real files. With no intermediate format, version control keeps working and there is nothing to synchronise.
  3. Visual where the data is visual. Coordinates, graphs and maps are edited by looking at them; text and numbers, with forms.
  4. Keep what you do not understand. The editor preserves the keys it does not know on save, so a field added by hand or by another system is never lost.
  5. Put warnings where the mistake happens. A warning on the right screen is worth more than a paragraph of documentation.
  6. Write it down for the next person. The moment someone else uses the tool, its undocumented conventions become bugs.
  7. It is debt with interest. The editor needs maintenance too: a new field in the game demands a new field in the editor, and some things are still not covered. Cinematics are still edited by hand, weapons are tuned in a separate in-game weapon studio, and the editor cannot show you how a change feels in the game, only that the data is consistent.

Conclusion​

None of this shows up in the trailer, but it is what lets one person with some help keep a game with 27 quests, 20 characters and 869 strings from collapsing. The editor does not make the game better by itself. It makes iterating cheap, and that is what ends up making the game better.

If you build a data-driven game, build the editor early, and make it edit the files you already have.

item.title: Making of Candelabra: a city-scale RTS built with Brakeza3D
item.description: How Candelabra, a city-scale RTS with civilians, traffic, police and a day/night cycle, was built on Brakeza3D, and which engine features it pushed into existence.
item.content:encoded:
For a while now, most of my time has gone into Candelabra: a real-time strategy game set in a dark, rain-soaked city carved up between street gangs. It is also the hardest stress test Brakeza3D has ever had. Every time the game asked for something the engine could not do, the engine grew a new feature.

This post is a tour of how the project came together, with screenshots from the current build.

The idea​

Candelabra is a city-sized RTS: you start with a handful of units, take over buildings, put workers to work, research upgrades and push into the districts held by the rival gangs. But the city is not a static map. Civilians walk the streets, traffic obeys traffic lights, the police react to violence, and a day/night cycle with weather runs on top of everything.

On top of the strategy layer there is a story. The city wakes up to a body hanging from a crane in the central plaza, and everybody has a theory. You play Vicente, an old pupil of the dead man, and you have to work out what really happened while four factions fight for the districts. I will not spoil more than that.

The rule I set from day one: the game is made with the engine's own tools, not with a fork of it. Everything in Candelabra is a scene, a model, a shader or a Lua script that any Brakeza3D user could also write.

Why Lua, and how much of the game is Lua​

The engine is C++17 and OpenGL 4.3, but almost the entire game lives in Lua scripts on top of the Brakeza3D bridge: the unit state machines, the enemy AI, the building and production queues, the economy, the quest and dialogue system, the police, the traffic, the HUD.

That is the reason the iteration speed has been good. Change a script, reload, and you are looking at the result. The C++ side only changed when the game hit a wall: a missing API, or a performance problem that no script could fix.

Seeing the whole city at once​

The first problem of an RTS set in a real city is how many things you need to draw. A top-down view means hundreds of buildings, cars, props and animated characters on screen simultaneously, plus the dynamic lights of windows, street lamps and vehicles.

Most of what you read in the 0.26.10 release notes was born here:

  • Shared GPU geometry and instancing, including skinned characters, because a crowd is the same few models repeated many times.
  • Shadow caster culling per light, so a lamp only pays for what it can actually light.
  • Emissive materials for neon signs and lit windows that ignore scene lighting.
  • Path costs for pathfinding, so units prefer streets over cutting through walls.

The deferred renderer does the rest: G-Buffer, ADS lighting with up to 64 point and 64 spot lights, PCF shadows, and a scene post-processing chain for the grading, fog and rain.

A living city​

The part that surprised me most is how much of the "game feel" comes from systems that are not strictly the game.

  • Traffic. Cars follow a directed lane graph with an IDM (intelligent driver model) for car-following, traffic lights, and yield rules at intersections. They brake for you if you walk in front of them.
  • Pedestrians. One single manager updates all the decorative civilians, so a thousand people on the streets is a matter of budget, not of one script per person.
  • Police and wanted level. Violence is published on an event bus. Police cars come from the station, agents get out and fight whoever caused the trouble, and if you keep escalating, the response escalates too.
  • Movement feel. Units accelerate and brake instead of snapping to speed, avoid each other with a predictive separation and smooth their paths, which is a big part of why a group of soldiers looks like a group and not like a spreadsheet.

The game starts here: ten units, a fog of war that only reveals what they see, and a city that keeps going whether you are watching or not.

Buildings, economy and the tech tree​

Buildings are picked straight from the city geometry. Click one and you get its actions, production queue and rally point.

Acquisition mode​

For the bigger picture there is an acquisition mode: a management view of the whole city where buildings are coloured by faction. A panel lists everything you own with its health, another shows the details of the selected building, and a third lists the neutral buildings in sight. Every row has a button to jump the camera straight to that building.

Places worth a visit​

Many buildings can be entered, and each one has its own personality: a casino, a nightclub, a Mexican restaurant, a strip club. Here are a few of them, seen from outside.

Tech tree​

Resources feed a tech tree with eight branches (economy, soldiers, snipers, workers, agitators, the hero, vehicles and streets). Upgrades chain together, and some unlock new abilities, like the Molotov cocktails of the agitators or their smoke bombs.

Characters, dialogue and a story you can talk to​

The city is full of people with something to say. Every NPC has a dialogue tree, quests are data files that the quest manager can chain, and phone messages arrive during the game to push the story forward. Dialogue scenes are staged with the character portraits and the camera, using the engine's UI widgets.

Everything here is data-driven: adding an NPC, a quest or a message means editing JSON, not touching code. That mattered a lot, because writing the lore turned out to be a job as big as the engineering.

The UI: widgets, atlases and live themes​

The whole HUD (minimap, resource counters, command card, alert panel, clock) is built from the engine's UI widgets, with the layout stored as JSON and edited inside Brakeza3D.

Its look comes from an atlas of UI images that can be re-cut and swapped. I also wired live UI themes and city styles that change while the game runs, which is great for experimenting with a direction before committing to it.

The Blender pipeline​

All the art goes through Blender: the city, the interiors, the vehicles and the characters (with animations from Mixamo). It used to be a pile of manual steps and every export was a chance to break something: an object at the wrong scale, an FBX with absolute texture paths, a missing animation.

I replaced it with one script that exports each asset from a preset, backs up the previous file, validates the FBX and compares it to the old version. Adding a new model to the game is now a one-liner, and that has been worth more than any optimisation.

What I learned​

  1. Build the game, and the engine follows. I never had a clear list of engine features at the start. I had a game that needed things.
  2. Tooling pays for itself. The profiler, the in-game debug panels, the weapon studio and the export scripts took time to write and saved much more.
  3. Measure first. Almost every performance hunch I had was wrong, and the profiler was right.
  4. Keep the game in scripts. It keeps the engine honest: if I cannot do something from Lua, other people cannot either.

What is next​

There is still a lot to do: balancing, more districts and interiors, more polish on the story. Many of the improvements made for Candelabra will keep landing in the engine releases, so everyone using Brakeza3D benefits.

If you want to follow along, the code is on GitHub and builds are on the downloads page. And if you are building something with Brakeza3D, I would love to see it.

Thanks for reading!

item.title: Brakeza3D 0.26.10: Instanced Rendering and Emissive Materials
item.description: Brakeza3D 0.26.10 release notes: instanced deferred rendering, shared GPU geometry, emissive materials, new audio backend, faster async loading and UI upgrades.
item.content:encoded:
Brakeza3D 0.26.10 is here! This release is all about performance and polish: a reworked renderer with instancing and shared GPU geometry, emissive materials, a brand-new audio backend, faster async loading, a much more capable UI system, path costs for pathfinding, and command-line parameters for automated runs.

Download for Linux and Windows:

  • https://github.com/rzeronte/brakeza3d/releases/tag/0.26.10
  • https://brakeza.com/downloads

✨ What's New​

Rendering Performance Overhaul​

The deferred renderer has been profiled and optimized end to end. Scenes with many copies of the same model are now dramatically cheaper.

  • Shared GPU geometry — every Mesh3D / Mesh3DAnimation created from the same model file shares its vertex buffers, with deduplicated index buffers
  • Instancing — an opaque render queue groups objects by model and draws them instanced in the G-Buffer, shadow and picking passes. Animated models too: bones are skinned in the vertex shader from a bone-matrix texture buffer
  • Shadow caster culling — each light only renders the casters inside its own frustum
  • State caches — FBO/program bind cache and a shared GL render-state cache remove redundant state changes; projection and view travel in a single CameraBlock uniform buffer

Emissive Materials​

Mesh3D objects can now glow with their own color, ignoring scene lighting: screens, neon signs, lamps, magic effects. Emission is off by default and adds no cost to scenes that do not use it.

local sign = Brakeza:getObjectByName("neon_sign")
sign:setEmissionEnabled(true)
sign:setEmissionIntensity(0.8)   -- 0 = lit normally, 1 = full self-illumination

Available in the object inspector, saved in scene files and fully scriptable.

New Audio Backend: miniaudio​

SDL2_mixer has been replaced by miniaudio, bundled as a single header — one dependency less to install on Linux.

  • Same Lua API as before (playSound, channels, Sound3D, ambience volume...)
  • WAV, MP3 and FLAC support, also for positional Sound3D sources
  • New setChannelPitch(channel, pitch) for engine RPM, Doppler and similar effects

Faster Async Loading​

  • Per-file load locks in the resource caches: the same file is never loaded twice in parallel
  • The compute thread pool is sized from the CPU core count
  • Deferrable jobs: work that has to wait no longer blocks a worker thread
  • Animated billboards get their own texture cache
  • Brakeza:getPendingJobsCount() and Brakeza:cancelPendingJobs() to drive loading screens and clean restarts; Components:Render():PreloadImage2D(path) warms up images before they are shown

UI System Upgrades​

The widget system takes a big step forward:

FeatureDetail
Fonts per widget and per elementAny .ttf / .otf; nested widgets inherit the parent's font
Word-wrapped textwrap, w, maxLines and lineSpacing on text elements
9-slice backgroundsbgSlice: frames whose corners keep their size when the panel is resized
Scrollable listsNew scroll element type
Pagers on toparrayPagerTop places a long list's pager above it
Resolution-aware textsetUIDesignResolution(w, h) and per-widget refHeight scale text with the window
New Lua helpersgetWidgetSize, invalidateWidget, invalidateAllWidgets, isUIScrollHovered

The UI Manager editor window gained the matching controls (font pickers, grouped sections...).

Related rendering helpers:

  • drawFillSubmesh(obj, submesh, r, g, b, a) — translucent highlight over a single submesh
  • TextWriter:measureTextWidthAtlas(text, scale) — measure batched atlas text to center or align it; atlas text now honors its tint color and blends correctly

Pathfinding — Path Costs​

Grid3D cells can now have a traversal cost. A* prefers cheaper cells, so units can favour sidewalks over roads or avoid dangerous areas without blocking them:

local grid = mesh:getGrid3D()
grid:fillCostFromImage("../assets/nav/roads.png", 128, 4.0)   -- roads cost 4
grid:setCellsCost({ 10, 12, 11, 12 }, 10.0)                   -- a temporary danger zone
print(grid:getCellCost(10, 12))

Grid world coordinates are now derived from the grid bounds.

Command-Line Parameters & Automation​

Projects can declare their own parameters and receive them from the command line — ideal for test scenarios, CI and benchmarks:

> brakeza3d.exe -p MyGame.json --set level=forest --set godMode=true --exit-after 300
  • --set key=value — passed to the project, declared in its cli_params (name, type, default)
  • --exit-after N — safety watchdog for headless runs
  • Brakeza:getCliParam(name) reads a parameter with its declared type
  • Brakeza:requestExit(code) closes the app with a process exit code

Scripting API Additions​

APIDescription
Brakeza:getDeltaTimeMS()Frame time in milliseconds (getDeltaTimeMicro() now really returns microseconds)
Brakeza:getImage3DAnimationByName()Typed access to animated billboards
BillboardAnimation:setTowardsCamera / setSize / setRenderFBFlat ground sprites, runtime resizing, render layer
Mesh3D:getModelFile() / getDiffuseTextureFile(i)Inspect the model and per-submesh textures
Input:isMouseInWindow()Know when the cursor leaves the window
ParticlesContext.PARTICLE_SIZE_SCALEParticle size multiplier

Profiler — Render Detail​

The Profiler adds exact per-frame draw call and triangle counters, CPU and real GPU time per render pass (GPU queries are optional, zero overhead when off), rolling history with median/P95/P99, and CSV export to compare a scene before and after an optimization.

Editor & Platform​

  • Scene badge in the project panel
  • Windows: the application icon is embedded in the executable (taskbar icon from the first frame)
  • New minimal UITest demo scene (UIWidgetsDemo.lua) showing a plain widget, a nested widget and an array with the sample widgets in assets/ui/

Bug Fixes​

  • Texture unit helpers only handled units 0–5 (higher units were bound onto the previous one)
  • UI widget editor now saves arrayPrefix
  • Black scene after a window resize (VAO name reuse in ground decals)
  • VRAM leak when destroying custom code shaders
  • Outline fill pass inheriting instancing flags
  • Editor grid disappearing
  • Two use-after-free crashes
  • Camera up vector computed from its own rotation

Documentation​

  • UI Widgets — new dedicated page: JSON format, element types, buttons, nested widgets, lists and pagination, scroll areas, 9-slice backgrounds, text scaling and the UI Manager editor
  • 3D Objects — Mesh3D model/texture methods, emission, shared geometry and instancing, animated billboards
  • Grid3D — movement costs
  • Scripting introduction — command-line parameters (--set, cli_params, --exit-after), requestExit, async loading helpers
  • Sound — miniaudio backend, supported formats, setChannelPitch
  • Text System — custom fonts with the glyph atlas, batched text and measureTextWidthAtlas
  • Editor — Profiler counters, GPU timing and CSV export
  • Download and Install — build from source updated: new Windows libraries package for 0.26.10 (no SDL2_mixer, exact MinGW build it needs) and the FFmpeg development packages on Linux

Thanks for testing Brakeza3D and sharing feedback ❤️

item.title: Brakeza3D 0.26.8: Positional Audio, Multi-Scene and Video
item.description: Brakeza3D 0.26.8 release notes: Sound3D positional audio, multi-scene support, video playback, the Swarm entity, multi-selection and editor improvements.
item.content:encoded:
Brakeza3D 0.26.8 is here! This release is packed with major new features: a full positional audio system, multi-scene support, video playback, a new Swarm entity, multi-selection across editor and scripting, and a large batch of rendering, physics, and editor improvements.

Download for Linux and Windows:

  • https://github.com/rzeronte/brakeza3d/releases/tag/0.26.8
  • https://brakeza.com/downloads

✨ What's New​

Sound3D — Positional Audio System​

A brand-new Sound3D scene object brings distance-based volume attenuation to the engine. Place ambient sounds anywhere in the world and let the engine handle volume falloff automatically based on the camera's distance.

  • Full inner/outer radius model: full volume inside innerRadius, linear fade to silence at outerRadius
  • Can be placed in the editor, saved in scene files, or created from Lua with ObjectFactory.Sound3D()
  • Global ambience volume — Components:Sound():setAmbienceVolume(percent) scales all Sound3D sources simultaneously, perfect for ducking world sounds during menus or cutscenes
  • Zone music crossfade: overlapping outer radii produce natural transitions with zero scripting
  • Background music mode: set innerRadius to a very large value for a non-positional track
local snd = ObjectFactory.Sound3D(
    "../assets/sounds/forest_ambient.wav",
    Vertex3D.new(0, 0, 0), 20, 80, 100
)
snd:setSoundLoop(true)
Brakeza:addObject3D(snd, "forest_ambient")

Multi-Scene System​

Scenes can now be loaded, shown, and hidden independently at runtime. Multiple scenes can coexist and be toggled without losing their state.

  • Brakeza:loadScene(path) / Brakeza:showScene(name) / Brakeza:hideScene(name)
  • Scene shader chains are properly saved and restored when a scene is hidden and re-shown — shaders that were disabled before hiding stay disabled on restore
  • Enables interior/exterior streaming: load interior scene, hide exterior, restore on exit

Video Player in Image2D​

Image2D objects can now play back video files directly inside the engine. Use the editor or Lua to assign a video source and control playback.

Swarm Entity​

A new Swarm object type for managing large groups of simple elements (particles, foliage, crowds) as a single scene node. Registered in the full serialization pipeline with editor inspector support.

Multi-Selection — Editor & Scripting​

Select multiple objects simultaneously in the viewport and operate on them as a group.

  • Ctrl + Left Click — toggle an object into/out of the current selection group
  • Ctrl + Left Drag — rectangle-select all objects inside the drawn area
  • Full scripting access via the new SelectionManager (extracted from ComponentRender), exposable to Lua
  • MultiSelectionDemo.lua updated with working examples

Rendering — Blob Shadows & Ground Circles​

Two new lightweight render primitives for real-time ground projection effects:

  • Blob shadows — circular soft-shadow decals projected onto the ground beneath objects
  • Ground circles — configurable radius/color rings for selection indicators, AoE zones, and UI feedback

Both are registered as GUI addons and fully scriptable from Lua.

Collider System Improvements​

  • Debug draw — visualize collision shapes in the viewport at runtime
  • Contact points — query per-frame collision contact data from Lua
  • resetColliderRotation() — snap a body's orientation back to identity without repositioning
  • Ghost body fix — ghost objects no longer interfere with dynamic simulation incorrectly
  • ColliderGUI refactored into its own standalone panel

Shadow Pass Optimization​

The shadow pass now skips meshes and scene regions that cannot cast shadows into the current light frustum, reducing GPU draw calls significantly in larger scenes.

Editor Improvements​

FeatureDetail
Solo window toggleFocus a single dockable panel, hiding the rest
Layout restoreLayouts are saved and restored across sessions
forceReloadLayoutForce-rebuild the dock layout from the current preset
`Ctrl + `` shortcutQuick toggle between CODING and DEFAULT layouts
Snap camera viewsInsert (front), Home (top), Page Up (side) — snaps camera to selected object

UIManager Improvements​

  • bgColor arrays: per-widget background color now accepts RGBA arrays in JSON
  • cacheable: false flag — bypass FBO caching for widgets that update position or alpha every frame (e.g. world-space unit overlays)
  • New scripting methods exposed: setWidgetAlpha, setWidgetPosition, showWidget, hideWidget, and more

TextWriter​

  • Tint color — writeTextAtlasCache now accepts a tint color parameter, enabling colored cached text without recreating the atlas
  • flushTextBatch() flushes the colored glyph batch correctly

Sound System — Per-Channel Control​

New Lua API for fine-grained channel control:

-- Pitch/frequency (engine RPM simulation, Doppler)
Components:Sound():setChannelFrequency(channel, freq)

-- Per-channel volume (independent of global setSoundsVolume)
Components:Sound():setChannelVolume(channel, vol)

-- 3D spatialization via angle + distance
Components:Sound():setChannelPosition(channel, angle, distance)

-- Query channel state
Components:Sound():isChannelPlaying(channel)
Components:Sound():isSoundPlaying("label")

Tools​

  • fbx_bounds.py — Python tool to extract vertex bounds from FBX files, useful for computing exact mesh positions after Blender export

Documentation​

Major documentation additions:

  • Sound3D — new dedicated API page covering positional audio, zone crossfade, ambience volume, and Lua methods
  • Sound System — expanded with per-channel control, isSoundPlaying, and setAmbienceVolume
  • Components API — UIManager widget system documented (9 methods)
  • 3D Objects — Image3DAnimation360 section added
  • Shaders System — pipeline order and execution steps documented
  • Keyboard Shortcuts — snap camera keys (Insert / Home / Page Up) added

Profiler — Expanded Diagnostics​

The built-in ImGui profiler gained a large set of new panels, turning it into a full runtime diagnostics tool:

PanelWhat it shows
Frame TimePer-frame ms plot with 120-frame rolling history
ComponentsPer-component pre/update/post timing breakdown with sparklines
Script DetailPer-Lua-script timing, toggled independently
CachesLive entry counts and memory usage for Image, Model, Animation, Script, and Scene caches
Frame BuffersAll active FBOs with their color/depth attachments and dimensions
OpenGL StatusCurrent GL state: bound program, bound FBO, active texture units, FBO/program switch counters per frame
Post-Processing ChainEnabled/disabled status and execution order of every scene shader in the chain
Thread PoolsActive tasks, pending tasks, pending callbacks, total processed, and a 120-frame throughput sparkline per pool
CollidersRuntime list of active physics bodies with mode, group, and AABB
System MemoryTotal and free RAM on Windows, Linux, and macOS via native OS APIs

FBO and GL program switch counters are incremented at the call site throughout the render pipeline, giving exact per-frame context switch counts with no estimation.

Bug Fixes & Maintenance​

  • Fixed GCC warnings in debug mode across multiple translation units
  • Fixed X11 + NVIDIA OpenGL window creation on Linux
  • Fixed Image2D size/position regression
  • Fixed bad dynamic_cast in core components
  • Removed RTS-specific demo widgets from engine examples, keeping only generic ones
  • Debian build setup scripts updated

This release marks a significant step forward in audio, scene management, and editor workflow. Thanks for testing Brakeza3D and sharing feedback ❤️

item.title: Brakeza3D Roadmap: Stability, Lua API and Documentation
item.description: Brakeza3D roadmap: stabilizing the engine, exposing 100% of its functionality to Lua, documenting the API, then desired mid and long-term features.
item.content:encoded:
First of all, thank you.

I want to take a moment to thank everyone who has emailed me and shown so much interest after the latest video about the Brakeza3D 0.26.2 release. The response from the community has been incredibly positive and motivating, and it truly means a lot to see so many people interested, testing the engine, and asking how they can use it or contribute.

About the roadmap​

One of the questions that keeps coming up in messages is:

What is the project's roadmap?

The answer is clear and honest:
The current priority is not to add lots of new features, but to stabilize and consolidate the project.

The main focus right now is:

  • Stabilizing the engine
  • Improving internal consistency
  • Exposing 100% of the engine’s functionality to LUA
  • Properly documenting that API

At the moment, the LUA API is still limited, and before expanding the engine with new capabilities, I want to make sure everything that already exists is:

  • accessible
  • stable
  • documented
  • maintainable

This step is essential to make the project truly usable in the long term.

Priorities for the coming months​

The priority order will be:

  1. Bug fixing
  2. Documenting the LUA API and the C++ core
  3. Desired features
  4. Long-term features

This order is intentional. An engine with many features but poor stability or documentation ends up being frustrating for users. I prefer building a solid foundation before accelerating development.

Desired features (mid-term)​

These are some improvements planned that will be implemented progressively:

  • Improve user experience in the interface
  • Enable geometry streaming for Mesh3D objects
  • Add a basic version of node-based geometry shaders

Many of these ideas come directly from community feedback, which helps a lot when deciding what actually brings value.

Long-term features (or subject to reconsideration)​

There are also deeper evolution paths that require analysis and experimentation before any decision is made:

  • Decouple OpenGL / Create a Vulkan backend
  • Explore alternative scripting language options
  • Change the project's license type

These decisions affect the architecture, philosophy, and long-term direction of the engine, so they will be evaluated carefully and with community feedback.

Thanks again​

To close, I want to repeat the most important thing:
thank you for the interest, feedback, and support.

This project keeps moving forward thanks to you.

Let’s keep going 🚀

item.title: Assets Hub Alpha: Share Lua Scripts and Shaders for Brakeza3D
item.description: Assets Hub alpha: a free portal, integrated into the Brakeza3D engine, to share, discover, rate and download community Lua scripts and shaders.
item.content:encoded:
Assets Hub Alpha Released 🚀​

We’re excited to announce the alpha release of Assets Hub, a new platform designed to expand and strengthen the Brakeza3D ecosystem.

Assets Hub is an integrated portal where the community can share, discover, and reuse scripts and shaders created by other Brakeza3D users. The main goal is to encourage collaboration, learning, and faster development through high-quality community-driven resources.

Deep Integration with Brakeza3D​

Assets Hub is directly integrated into the Brakeza3D engine. The engine now includes a built-in client that allows users to:

  • Log in to their Assets Hub account
  • Browse community-created assets
  • Vote and rate resources
  • Download scripts and shaders created by third parties

All of this happens without leaving the engine, keeping the workflow fast and seamless.

Web Portal for Asset Management​

Assets Hub is also available as a web platform at:

https://hub.brakeza.com/

From the web interface, creators can upload, update, and manage their assets, making it easy to maintain and showcase their contributions to the community.

Alpha Status​

Assets Hub is currently in alpha, which means it is still under active development. Features, workflows, and APIs may change in the coming weeks as we iterate based on feedback.

This early stage is a great opportunity for the community to test the platform and help shape its future.

Free and Ad-Free​

Assets Hub is a free service, with no advertisements and no hidden costs. It is built to support the Brakeza3D community and promote open sharing and collaboration.
